This ruler gave territory to Poland in the Peace of Zapoli and land to the Swedes in the truce of Ilyusa. He had St. Philip killed because Philip refused to bless him and condemned this leader's oprichina. This monarch stripped the aristocratic princes and Muscovian boyars of their power. This ruler greatly expanded Russian territory, including conquering Kazan and Astrakhan. This monarch destroyed Novgorod and killed his own son. Name this first Tsar of All Russia, whose moniker refers to his fearsomeness, not his cruelty.

Cryptozoologists believe that the Ropen of Papua New Guinea is a member of this order. Rhamphorhynchoids and Ctenochasmatoids were basal species of this order; the basal species with longer tails evolved to a later suborder with shorter tails, including Quetzalcoatlus. Most species in this order ate fish and were slow bipedal runners with hollow bones; often wings were attached to their hind legs and fourth finger. Scientists think that species in this order were adept flyers, not just gliders. Name this extinct order of flying reptiles.

This country was first conquered by Pedro de Valdivia, and the Battle of Chacabuco occurred during this country's war of independence. This nation gained control of the nitrate rich portions of the Atacama when it won the War of the Pacific over Peru and Bolivia. While Bernardo O'Higgins became its first president, Richard Nixon notoriously ordered the overthrow of a Marxist president of this country. Name this South American country in which Salvador Allende was overthrown by Augusto Pinochet in its capital, Santiago.

This conflict saw the victor of the Battle of Towton take the throne. Richard Neville gained the epithet "kingmaker" after deposing two kings during this conflict, which began with the battles of St. Albans and Northampton. One king's reign during this war was briefly interrupted by Henry VI. This conflict was sparked by Henry Bolingbroke seizing the throne from Richard II and culminated at the Battle of Bosworth Field. Name this conflict between the houses of York and Lancaster, both represented by its namesake flowers.

This project began when John Marshall and James Madison formed a committee for its construction. The interior of this monument is granite and gneiss and the exterior is marble from Maryland. This monument was designed by Robert Mills but his plan was changed to include a pointed top. Fifty flags surround the base of this monument which stands at the opposite end of a reflection pool from the Lincoln Memorial. Name this obelisk located in the national mall in Washington D.C. Named for the first president of the United States.

This ruler invaded Iberia during the Peninsular War, which saw the Second of May uprising. Along with Alexander I of Russia, this ruler signed the Treaty of Tilsit. This leader's army routed Hungarian forces in the Battle of Marengo, and he devised the Continental System to curb British influence after suffering a defeat to Horatio Nelson at the Battle of Trafalgar. This figure's escape from Elba resulted in the Hundred Days until he lost at Waterloo. Name this first emperor of France.

This president was called a bigamist because he married his wife before her divorce was final. This leader's cabinet was rearranged during the Peggy Eaton Affair. His being called a "jackass" led to the donkey being adopted as a symbol of the Democratic Party. This president had to contend with the "nullification crisis" in South Carolina and sought to annul the Second Bank of the United States. This man had earlier gained popular support after winning the Battle of New Orleans. Name this seventh president, nicknamed "Old Hickory."

One battle during this war was the last conflict in which a reigning British monarch led their troops in war. In addition to the Battle of Dettingen, this war also saw the Duke of Cumberland's forces lose Tournai to Maurice de Saxe at the Battle of Fontenoy. This war was sparked after Charles VI's failure to override Salic law with the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713, and the invasion of Silesia by Frederick Wilhelm II. Identify this war ended by the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle in 1748, fought over Maria Theresa's right to accede to her country's throne.

After this woman was mentioned in a John McCain campaign ad, she created her own campaign video featuring her in a leopard print swimsuit. She sang "I can make you nice and naughty... Even though the gods are crazy" in her song "Stars Are Blind." She won a Razzie Award for her role as Cristabel in The Hottie and the Nottie. This woman says to "always walk around like you have an invisible tiara" in her book Confessions of an Heiress. With her dog Tinkerbell and friend Nicole Richie, she appeared on the TV show The Simple Life. For 10 poitns, name this hotel-chain heiress.

This country's trade minister resigned after just eight days following remarks threatening to give a newspaper reporter radiation poisoning. Moody's recently cut this non-American country's credit rating score and a student from this country drowned after falling over Niagara Falls. An airport controller from this country blogged about the movement of Air Force One, for which Prime Minister Noda apologized. A tsunami struck this country, including the island of Honshu, home to its capitol and Mt. Fuji. Name this Asian country with capital at Tokyo.

The first of these conflicts began with the Mamertines trying to seize control of trade routes in Sicily, and Numidia's invasion of Hasdrubal's territory sparked the third of these conflicts. One force was defeated at the Battles of the Trebia and Cannae during the second of these conflicts, while Scipio Africanis ended the longest of these wars at the Battle of Zama. During the second of these conflicts, Hannibal crossed the Alps into Italy. Name this series of three wars between the Roman Republic and the city of Carthage.

This leader abolished the Poor Law while serving as Chancellor of the Exchequer under Ramsey MacDonald. He sent Robert Hodgson as an ambassador to Francisco Franco's government, but ultimately ended up resigning after his failed Norwegian campaign. This leader gave his "Peace in Our Time" speech after he signed the Munich Agreement that ceded the Sudetenland to Germany as part of his policy of appeasement with the Nazis. Name this British Prime Minister who preceded Churchill.

This man ordered the execution of Robert Ambrister and Alexander Arbuthnot for spying during his military career. This president repeatedly advocated abolishing the Electoral College in his addresses to Congress, and he fired his entire cabinet after the Peggy Eaton affair. His Vice President resigned during the Nullification crisis, to which this president responded with the Force Bill, and this president fought Nicholas Biddle over the existence of the Second Bank of the United States. Name this seventh President, nicknamed "Old Hickory."

The Bosporan Kingdom was annexed during this emperor's reign, and he married the ex-wife of a later emperor, Poppea Sabina. This emperor built a barge that would collapse on the water in an attempt to kill his mother, Agrippina the Younger. This man's death and Galba's ascension to the throne marked the beginning of the Year of the Four Emperors, and this man's rule saw Suetonius Paullinus crush a revolt led by the queen of the Iceni, Boudicca, in Britannia. Name this Roman emperor that supposedly fiddled while Rome burned.

This empire experienced a 19-year interregnum after the reign of Conrad IV. It allowed one region to levy capital punishment through Vehmic courts, and it claimed its legitimacy through the doctrine of translatio imperii. Though it was not officially dissolved until the abdication of Francis II in 1806, its rule was decentralized by the Peace of Westphalia. Name this empire ruled by Otto I, a collection of mostly German states and the nominal successor to an earlier empire centered in Italy.

A political party in this country massacred people in a former high school called S-21, or Tuol Sleng, and overthrew Norodom Sihanouk ["sigh"-an-ouk]. That party was named after an ancient empire in this country, which was ruled by Jayavarman II and led by a man who identified himself as "Brother Number One." The Ba Chúc Massacre led to war between Vietnam and the Pol Pot-led Khmer Rouge of this nation. Name this country where the ancient city of Angkor Wat lies to the north of Phnom ["Puh-NOM"] Penh.

Sir Charles Napier led a fleet to attack the Finnish coast in this conflict's Baltic Campaign. Aleksandr Menshikov was defeated during this war's Battle of the Alma and in the Battle of Inkerman. During this war, the Earl of Cardigan ordered a cavalry charge at the Battle of Balaclava. Czar Alexander II agreed to remove all military forces from Russia's Black Sea Coast after this conflict. Name this war fought between Russia and a coalition of France, Great Britain, and the Ottoman Empire over a namesake Black Sea peninsula.

A Supreme Court decision upholding this practice relied on a Pennsylvania state decision in Kneedler v. Lane and heavily cited Emerich de Vattel's The Law of Nations. U.S. V. O'Brien determined laws against one method of protesting this practice to be illegal, and when introduced in the U.S., it could be avoided by paying a $300 fee or hiring a substitute, leading to a riot in New York City. Vietnam War protesters opposed this practice by burning the cards requiring them to participate in it. Name this action, where people are required to serve in the military.

Thomas Wolsey. This king appointed Thomas Cranmer as Archbishop of Canterbury, and Cranmer subsequently assisted this king's religious reforms as he seized the monasteries and declared himself head of the Church of England. Identify this English monarch who famously had six wives.

During this battle, a Breton division broke rank on the left flank, but their opponent's brothers Leofwyne and Gyrthe were still killed. One side at this battle used warriors called housecarls, who unwisely left the protection of their shield wall in pursuit of retreating foes. This battle, which was preceded by the defeat of Harold Hardrada at the battle of Stamford Bridge, ended when the English commander was shot through the eye with an arrow. Identify this 1066 battle at which William the Conqueror defeated Harold Godwinson, taking control of England.

John B. Kendrick proposed an investigation into this incident. This incident led to the ruling in McGrain v. Daugherty that Congress could compel testimony, and it began after Edwin Denby transferred control of some of his assets. Edward Doheny was acquitted for his involvement in this event, but Harry Sinclair was fined $100,000 for his involvement with Mammoth Oil in relation to this scandal. Identify this political scandal in which Warren Harding's Secretary of the Interior Albert Fall sold the right to drill in naval oil reserves for a profit.

A widely published photograph of this man doing domestic work was taken by Margaret Bourke White. This author of The Story of My Experiments With Truth gave one class of citizens the nickname Harijan, or "Children of God." This man wore homespun clothing to protest against foreign textiles. This leader led a march to the coastal city of Dandi to protest a British tax on salt; that action was one example of his practice of Satyagraha. Identify this Indian nationalist leader, assassinated in 1948, famous for practicing nonviolent civil disobedience.

One resident of this city has his estate taken over by Captain Face and the con man Subtle. One character who hosts a party in this city thinks about marrying Peter Walsh. This setting of The Alchemist and Mrs. Dalloway is the site of an opium den where one character is confronted by Sibyl Vane's brother. This setting of The Picture of Dorian Gray was described in 1802 in a William Wordsworth poem, and is home to Tellson's Bank and the Manette House in A Tale of Two Cities. Name this city on the Thames River.

At the age of twelve, this man was sent to the court of Emperor Honorius as a hostage, while his people received Flavius Aetius in return. After Ruga's death, this man became co-ruler with his brother. This man threatened to sack the Eastern Roman Empire after the bishop of Margus desecrated his people's burial sites, and this man's conquest of the Western Roman Empire was ended after an alliance between Rome and Theodoric's Visigoths halted this man at Chalons ["SHAH"-loan]. Name this "Scourge of God" that ruled the Huns.

A cornerstone laid for this building was removed two years later after it was redesigned. Chamfered corners begin on this building's 20th floor, making the rest consist of 8 isosceles triangles. When completed, this structure will stand 1776 feet tall, and Conde Nast is a planned major tenant of this building. Designed by Daniel Libeskind, this structure surpassed the Empire State Building as the tallest in New York in April, 2012 and is planned to be the third tallest building in the world. Name this unfinished skyscraper being built at the former Ground Zero in Manhattan.

One provision of this agreement allowed for Lithuania to annex Memmel, and another gave Rwanda and Burundi to Belgium. This treaty limited one signatory's army to 15,000 men, and China rejected it because it did not receive Shandong. Vittorio Orlando was not able obtain Fiume, causing resentment in Italy. The terms of this treaty were resisted by a coalition led by Henry Cabot Lodge, leading to its rejection in the United States. Identify this treaty in which Georges Clemenceau forced war guilt and unreasonable reparations on Germany, that ended World War I.

One of this ruler's generals was sent to overthrow the barbarian Gelimer and won the Battles of Tricamarum and Ad Decimum. He was called a "million year old demon" in The Secret History by Procopius, and the Blue and Green factions at a chariot race turned into a rebellion against him, the Nika Revolt. This emperor's general Belisarius reconquered much of the Western Roman Empire and this emperor built the Hagia Sofia in his capital city. Name this "Great" ruler of the Byzantine Empire who created a namesake law code.

This man founded a magazine called The Commoner, and he was a speaker on the Chautauqua circuit in support of Prohibition. This man, who delivered a speech titled "The Paralyzing Influence of Imperialism," later resigned as Secretary of State to protest Woodrow Wilson's handling of the Lusitania incident. As a lawyer, this man argued against Clarence Darrow in the Scopes Trial. Name this loser of the presidential elections of 1896, 1900, and 1908 who delivered the "Cross of Gold" speech.

This ruler reformed the government of Livonia due to its financial woes, and he also repressed the Streltsy. This ruler changed New Year's Day from September 1st, and he cheated on his wife Eudoxia with Anna Mons. This ruler put a naval base at Taganrog to help him capture Azov. This czar's reforms included changes in court etiquette and a tax on beards, which he saw as antiquated. This czar defeated Charles XII at Poltava, allowing his country to gain large tracts of land from Sweden. Identify this Czar that westernized Russia and founded a new capital at St. Petersburg.

One event in this conflict was the genocide of supposed subverters in the Bodo League Massacre. Many civilians were killed at No Gun Ri during this conflict, and Matthew Ridgway took command after another general was relieved for suggesting that the US invade China. This war saw UN troops cross the Pusan Perimeter and land on Green Beach during the assault on Inchon, and the DMZ was established at the 38th parallel after this war. Name this war fought on a namesake peninsula, where UN forces were commanded by Douglas MacArthur.

This empire's Köprülü era occurred when royal advisers from the namesake family dominated the government, and its Tulip period included renovations of its ruler's residence at the Topkapi Palace. This empire won the Battle of Mohács [mow-HOCH], and Bursa was once its capital. In the Auspicious Incident, it disbanded its Janissary forces, and it controlled the entire Balkans under Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. Identify this empire of Asia Minor that ruled from its capital at Istanbul.

In 200 people are descended from this man, and he used mounted archers and faked retreats to fool foes into traps. Name this unifier of the Mongol Tribes whose grandson Kublai ruled the largest contiguous empire in history.

This event began when Edward Garrick attempted to collect a non-existent debt. Hugh White believed that his position before this incident was jeopardized, which led him to call for reinforcements. This event took place outside the Old State House, and Josiah Quincy II and John Adams defended its perpetrators in court. This event began after one group had thrown snowballs at another, and Crispus Attucks was its first casualty. Identify this event in which British soldiers opened fire on agitated colonists, killing five of them.

This man created the first accurate maps of the coast of Newfoundland, and he also improved the accuracy of maps of the Pacific Northwest. This man was originally sent on his most famous voyage to observe a transit of Venus, and he was killed while repairing his ships in Hawaii, which he visited on his third voyage. His second voyage saw him circumnavigate islands he discovered to prove they were not connected to a southern landmass. Identify this British explorer who was the first European to reach eastern Australia and New Zealand.

The Merville Gun Battery was captured in this event's Operation Tonga. Miles Dempsey led a force that advanced to Bayeux [buy-YOU] in one part of this battle, and at another location, a British force failed to capture Caen. Though he was away when it began, Erwin Rommel planned the defenses in this battle. Fighting in it occurred at Gold Beach and Sword Beach, and Americans assaulted a heavily fortified Atlantic seawall on Omaha Beach. Identify this amphibious assault on Normandy that opened a second front against Germany.

This civilization's warriors used shields called chimallis, and it had an elite military order called the "shorn ones." This civilization, which launched the Flower Wars for religious ceremonies, formed a Triple Alliance between its major cities, including Texcoco and Tlacopan, and its capital city was located in the middle of a lake. This civilization's downfall occurred after Hernan Cortes captured its last emperor, Montezuma II, in Tenochtitlan. Name this Mesoamerican civilization whose people worshipped gods such as Quetzalcoatl.

To open this battle, one army made an atypical charge due to the large number of their opponent's archers. Cynaegirus [si-nay-GYR-us] died during this battle while pulling an enemy boat towards shore. Sparta did not participate in this battle because their troops were delayed celebrating Carneia, and before this battle, the two sides sat in a five day stalemate. This battle's losers were commanded by Datis and Artaphernes. Identify this battle where Athenians and their allies stopped Darius I of Persia from invading Greece, after which Pheidippides ran 26 miles to notify the city of victory.

This ruling cited Strader v. Grahm, and it began with a lawsuit against Eliza Emerson. In this decision, the Court gave itself jurisdiction based on the Privileges and Immunities Clause, and it ruled that states could not grant American citizenship. Benjamin Curtis' dissent in this case cited the Northwest Ordinance, but the majority opinion, written by Roger Taney, overturned the Missouri Compromise. Name this 1857 Supreme Court case that ruled slaves were not citizens.

The Pyidaungsu Hluttaw recently passed a law that raised this nation's public sector wages, and recent allowances for international investment have caused its Kyat currency to strengthen. This nation recently began allowing opposition figures to be pictured in print media. The National League for Democracy boycotted this country's 2010 elections, and Thein Sein succeeded Than Shwe as its president. Aung San Suu Kyi is an activist in, what Southeast Asian nation that has seen rapid democratic reforms?

This man's commander Marshal de Luxembourg won him victories at Steenkerque and Neerwinden. He removed Nicolas Fouquet as finance minister, allowing him to issue new taxes such as the aides, and his armies overran the Franche-Comté during the War of Devolution. This king's grandson Philip became king of Spain, and this man revoked the political and religious freedoms of Huguenots in his Edict of Fontainebleau [fon-tain-BLEW]. He took the throne at age 5 and reigned for 72 years. Identify this Sun King of France who built the palace of Versailles.

The Supreme Court upheld the application of this process to corporations in Flint v. Stone Tracy Co. Henry Addington stopped the first attempted implementation of this process in Britain. First introduced in 1862 for the Civil War, it was reintroduced in the Wilson-Gorman Tariff. This process was struck down by Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust. George W. Bush lowered this policy's top marginal rate to 35%. Name this action, legalized on the Federal level by 16th Amendment, whereby the government takes a part of the money you earn.

One person involved in this initiative who urged cabinet members to read Giovanni Gentile's "The Corporate State" was Hugh Johnson. This initiative, which included the passage of the John Collier-supported Indian Reorganization Act, included a program represented by a Blue Eagle and the phrase "We Do Our Part," the National Recovery Administration, and much of it was passed during the "First Hundred Days" of its main proponent's term. Name this series of economic programs created by Franklin Delano Roosevelt to combat the Great Depression.

Pepi II ruled this polity for 94 years, and some of its early tombs are called Mastabas. This empire's capital was moved for a time to Avaris, and it built temples at Beit el-Wali and Abu Simbel. This civilization's capitals included Memphis and Thebes, and their history contains three interregnums called "Intermediate Periods". Led by men such as Menes and Khufu, name this ancient civilization on the Nile River, responsible for building the tombs in the Valley of the Kings as well as the Pyramids of Giza.

Queenston Heights in this war's Niagara Campaign, and, although one side won the Battle of Bladensburg, they failed to capture Ft. McHenry. The Battle of New Orleans occurred two weeks after the Treaty of Ghent ended this war. Name this war between the US and Great Britain, named for the year in which it began.

Some of these people's burial grounds include Jelling and Brika, and this group won the Battle of Maldon. The Varangian Guard was composed of these peoples, and their rapid expansion has been attributed to Islamic interference with trade routes. A man named Rurik from these people established the Kievan Rus', and another, Rollo, conquered Normandy. These peoples colonized the Faeroe Islands, and later colonized Vinland and Greenland. Identify these people from Scandinavia who were known as vicious sea raiders in Medieval Europe.

A battery at Nicodemus Hill bombarded one position during this battle where John Sedgwick's advance from the East Woods was repulsed. A.P. Hill stopped Ambrose Burnside's attack on a stone bridge at this battle, before which one side's plans were found wrapped around cigars. Intense fighting in this battle occurred at Miller's Cornfield and at a sunken road that was named for the carnage that occurred there, Bloody Lane. Abraham Lincoln announced the Emancipation Proclamation after, what battle in Maryland, the bloodiest single day of the Civil War?

According to Baha'u'llah, these beings are people who "have consumed...all human traits and limitations." The Chayot Ha Kodesh are the highest rank of these according to Maimonides, while the Thrones and Seraphim belong to the highest order of the Pseudo-Dionysian hierarchy. One of these beings named Moroni gave the golden plates to Joseph Smith. The birth of John the Baptist was foretold to Zechariah by one of these named Gabriel, who also told Mary of the coming birth of Jesus. Satan is a fallen one of, what spirits who often serve as divine messengers?

This man withdrew his country's delegates to the EEC, precipitating the Empty Chair Crisis, but he later became a major figure in the drafting of the Treaty of Rome. This man pushed for the development of nuclear weapons, leading to successful tests in 1960, and he supported the Évian Accords to stop a war against the FLN and allow independence for Algeria. He survived the Generals' Putsch, and was largely responsible for the creation of France's 5th Republic. Identify this leader of the Free French, the namesake of Paris' main airport.
Charles André Joseph Marie de Gaulle

In this US election, Champ Clark failed to win the Democratic nomination because he was seen as a "Wall Street" candidate. The death of James Sherman left one candidate in this election without a running mate, and one of its issues was acceptance of the Payne-Aldrich Tariff. One candidate carried just Utah and Vermont as his party had split after it rejected a more popular candidate who instead ran for the "Bull Moose" Party. Identify this election in which Woodrow Wilson defeated Theodore Roosevelt and William Taft.

In 1983, this man formed the Revolutionary Bolivarian Movement-200, and he led a failed 1992 attempt to overthrow Carlos Andres Perez. This man survived a 2002 coup and a general strike that same year that crippled his nation's oil industry, and a 2004 recall referendum that was defeated. Despite travelling to Cuba for treatment for Colon cancer, this man defeated Henrique Capriles to win a fourth term as president. Name this long-serving president of Venezuela, an outspoken critic of the United States.

Before this battle, Lewis "Moses" Rose fled in fear, and James Neill gave up command of one force. One commander was killed while sitting in his bed, and James Fannin attempted to provide reinforcements from Goliad prior to this battle. William Travis became sole commander of his garrison at this battle when Jim Bowie fell ill. Identify this siege at which Mexican troops under Santa Anna besieged, assaulted, and massacred a force fighting for Texan independence.

"fallen cold and dead," was written as an elegy for Abraham Lincoln. Name this American author of "Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking", who included such poems as "O Captain! My Captain!" in Leaves of Grass.

During this period, a breakaway republic was set up on the island of Ezo and defeated at the Battle of Hakodate. The Ouetsu Reppan Domei was formed from supporters of the Aizu during this period, following the end of the Boshin War. This period's government was set up in the Charter Oath, and its reforms included banning samurai from carrying swords in public. Name this period of government that, after the Tokugawa Shogunate, rapidly modernized Japan under a namesake emperor.

This man was seasick during the battle of Naulochus, and he helped Aulus Hirtius win the battle of Mutina. Caepio and Murena unsuccessfully attempted to assassinate this emperor, who created the Urban Cohort. Marcus Agrippa was this man's favorite general, and his third wife Livia Drusilla bore his stepson and heir, Tiberius. Varrus lost three of his legions at the Battle of the Teutoberg Forest, and in part with Lepidus, he formed the 2nd triumvirate. Name this first emperor of Rome who took power after defeating Mark Antony at the Battle of Actium.

Johann Gotzkowsky built a silk factory for this ruler. He wrote the pamphlet The Anti-Machiavel, in which he argued against absolutism, and he reorganized his military tactics to include disciplined units relying on the oblique order of battle. This ruler signed, with Peter III, the Peace of Hubertusburg, and he defied the pragmatic sanction. He carried on a long correspondence with Voltaire. Name this monarch who unified most of his territory by partitioning Poland, an enlightened absolutist who acquired Silesia for his Kingdom of Prussia.

Endangered Species Act. At an exhibition of household appliances, this American engaged in the Kitchen Debate with Nikita Khrushchev, and his attempt to end the Vietnam War with secret bombings in Cambodia was exposed by the Pentagon Papers. Identify this US President who resigned due to the Watergate Scandal.

This man ruled a writ of error needs to have a citation in Bailiff v. Tipping. This man participated in the peace talks that ended the Quasi War with France, where he was involved in the XYZ affair. This man stopped states from invalidating contracts in Dartmouth College v. Woodward, and he broke up monopolies by affirming the Federal Government's ability to regulate commerce in Gibbons v. Ogden. This man's most famous opinion established the principle of Judicial Review. Name this longest serving Supreme Court Chief Justice who wrote the opinion in Marbury v. Madison.

This man's political career began with a defeat of Anastasia Garcia for his state's 111th House District. His memoir "An American Son" recounts his nearly 20 percentage point victory in the Republican primary over the then- governor of the state he represents. In June 2012, the primary legislative goal of this man who defeated Charlie Crist in that primary was co-opted by an executive order, preventing him from presenting a conservative alternative to the DREAM Act. Name this Florida Senator, the son of Cuban immigrants.

Hamilton Jordan participated in negotiations to resolve this event, and it was ended with the signing of the Algiers Accords. Ebrahim Asgharzadeh planned this event, which was carried out mostly by students. Eight soldiers died when a helicopter and airplane crashed during a failed attempt to end this event, Operation Eagle Claw, and this event started when Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi sought medical treatment in the US. Identify this 444 day incident in which 52 Americans were held hostage after a breakin of the Embassy in Tehran.

The first charge of this battle was made in tight formations to counter the opposing general's preference for massed short range musket barrages. Mistaking casualty trains for a retreat, one side ordered a series of cavalry charges at the enemy center under Marshal Ney, but those troops failed to spike the enemy cannons. This battle's winners were helped by wet ground, which delayed its start and allowed time for Prussians under General Blücher to arrive and seal this battle's outcome. Name this battle, the Duke of Wellington's final defeat of Napoleon Bonaparte in Belgium.

This man's reign ended when he died at the Battle of Massagetae, and his forces won the Battle of Opis, leading to the capture of Sippar. This emperor created a highly efficient postal system for his kingdom based on relay stations called Chapar Khaneh, and his provinces were watched over by his Satraps, who acted as governors. Cambyses II succeeded this emperor, who typically allowed locals of conquered lands to keep their religions and customs, such as the captive Jews whom he permitted to return home. Identify this King of Persia who conquered Lycia, Media, and Babylon.

This event began following a misinformation campaign named Operation Anadyr. George Anderson commanded a force including the USS Essex and Gearing during this event, in which Rudolf Anderson's Lockheed UF-2 was shot down. This event prompted the installation of the Red Line between two countries involved in it, and it was resolved after the US agreed to remove missiles from Italy and Turkey. Name this 1962 diplomatic confrontation between the US and Soviet Union over the deployment of nuclear weapons in Cuba.

This ruler took a world tour called the "Eastern Journey" while a prince, and his Prime Minister Pyotr Stolypin helped him curb liberal forces in local governments. This ruler was advised by Sergei Witte, and his navy lost the Battle of Tsushima Straits in the Russo-Japanese War. He gave nominal power to the Duma after a rebellion against him. This ruler's family was advised by the mystical Rasputin, and he was forced to flee to Yekaterinburg by Soviet forces. Identify this last Czar who was deposed and later killed in the Russian Revolution.

Cartagena Manifesto, and he broke with José de San Martín at the Guayaquil [guay-ah-KEEL] Conference. This man won the Battle of Boyacá, liberating Colombia, and he won the Battle of Carabobo in his own country. Name this Venezuelan revolutionary, namesake of a country with capitals at Sucre and La Paz.

A political cartoon in opposition to this bill depicted its author charming snakes, one of which is labeled "South America". Joshua Giddings and Salmon P. Chase argued against this law in their "Appeal of the Independent Democrats in Congress to the People of the United States." This bill advocated concepts attributed to Lewis Cass, and the debate over it destroyed the Whig Party. Sponsored by Stephen Douglass, identify this piece of legislation that opened all U.S. Territories to "Popular Sovereignty" and caused one of its namesakes to become "Bleeding."

Baldwin of Exeter raised 3,000 volunteers for this conflict, and its Battle of Arsuf led to the occupation of Jaffa. Guy of Lusignan quickly remarried to maintain power after his wife died during it, and he helped capture Acre. Philip II of France withdrew from this war rather than work with Richard the Lionheart. Earlier in the war, Frederick Barbarossa had drowned while attempting to cross a river in Turkey. Identify this war where European forces tried to recapture Jerusalem from Saladin.

One of these events occurred after Samuel Maharero of the Harero people led a revolt against German rule in Namibia. Another of these events occurred in 1995 in the village of Srebrenica [sre-breh-NEET-sa]. During World War I, Ottomans started one of these events in Armenia, and another occurred after Juvénal Habyarimana was killed, sparking the Hutu ethnic group to massacre the Tutsi minority in Rwanda. Identify these events such as the Holocaust, which involve large scale killing of an ethnic group.

His father claimed descent from Poseidon, and his mother was related to Solon. After his father's death, his mother married her uncle. This sounds like a Greek play, but it was reality for this philosopher. For 10 points \-- name this man whose most famous pupil described him as a man "whom it is blasphemy in the base even to praise," and who led the Academy.

A city founded in 1827, on April 15, 1865, Union general James H. Wilson would capture it in the last military battle of the Civil War east of the Mississippi. For 10 points -- name this city on the Chattahoochee River opposite Phenix City, Alabama, that shares its name with the capital city of Ohio.

This experimental, apolitical literary journal, edited by Wallace Henry Thurman, lasted one issue, November 1926, but influenced the Harlem Renaissance. In gemstones, it is a rapidly changing flash of color caused by dispersion. For 10 points -- name the "object" which prehistoric man "created" by using pyrite and flint.

Just 70% of the size of Washington, DC, this island's population of about 800 is decreasing, probably because its phosphate resources are near depletion and all the workers are employees of a phosphate mining company. For 10 points \-- name this Indian Ocean island, that is trying to create a tourism industry, which might be popular in late December.

This upstanding New York citizen donated the block and tackle used to build Trinity Church. He refused to attack a Dutch ship, leading to his killing gunner William Moore. His ships included the Antonio, the Adventure Galley, and the captured Armenian vessel, Que-dagh Merchant. For 10 points -- name this legendary pirate whose buried treasure is mentioned in Poe's The Gold Bug.

He has been the subject of biographies, historical fiction, and studies of saint's lives. The end of Ken Follett's novel Pillars of the Earth details the circumstances of his death. For 10 points -- name this meddlesome priest, whose death is chronicled in T.S. Eliot's lyric play Murder in the Cathedral.

In The Vicomte de Bra-ge-lonne, they continue their adventures, but meet their deaths. However, a story that had originally been planned as part of this novel was instead published separately, in which Fouquet [foo-KAY], Superintendent of Finance, foils their plans. For 10 points -- name these "heroes" created by Alexandre Dumas père.

Born in Switzerland in 1712, he was abandoned in Geneva when his father was exiled, and he later abandoned five of his own illegitimate children by Thérèse Levasseur. The librettist for the operas Les Muses Ga-lantes and Le De-vin du Village \-- for 10 points -- name this Enlightenment philosopher, author of the Political Treatises.

It originated with the union of the families of Ar-nulf, the bishop of Metz, and Pepin of Landon, the mayor of the palace in Aus-tra-sia. Name this dynasty which was prominent from the 700s to the 900s, whose family members included \-- for 10 points -- Charles the Bald, Lothair I, and Louis the German, and whose name comes from Charles Martel.

Helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson was awarded the Soldier's Medal 30 years after this March 16, 1968, event. This award is given to those who risk their lives where an opposing army is not involved, as when Thompson risked friendly fire to save civilian lives. For 10 points -- name this massacre which resulted in a court martial for Lieutenant William Calley.

A treason conviction not only caused the forfeit of one's lands to the king, but one's descendants would also forfeit property or assets inherited by title. The Constitution, though, forbids the issuing of such bills. For 10 points -- name this bill, mentioned in Article III, in which death sentences after a treason or felony conviction result in complete loss of civil and political rights.

Born in Rutland, Vermont, he became a blacksmith in Grand Detour, Illinois, but sold out to his partner, Major Leonard Andrus, and moved to Moline. In Moline, he began using imported English steel to make plows better suited to the soils of the prairie. What inventor's name is attached to a major US manufacturer of farm equipment?

After a statue was removed, it was transformed into a Christian church. Structural changes were made by the time that the Turks seized it in 1458, and turned it into a mosque two years later. And in 1687 a Venetian invasion caused a powder magazine to blow up, destroying the center of the building. For 10 points -- name the building from which Lord Elgin appropriated statues.

Given to the Smithsonian in 1907, it was originally presented to Major George Armstead. Sulfur bleaching agents and an ammonia-based cleaning solution have damaged this item, which has also had pieces of it snipped for souvenirs and which is missing one of its fifteen stars, given to an unknown politician. For 10 points -- name this 30-by-42 foot flag taken from Fort McHenry.

The chief architects of this 18th century movement were preachers like William Tennent, George Whitefield, and Jonathan Edwards. It led to a religious revival in the American colonies and ended in a bitter argument with the Calvinists. Name this popular upsurge in religious feeling.

This British economist and cleric influenced the thinking of Charles Darwin on natural selection as the driving force of evolution. For 10 points -- name the author of Essay on the Principle of Population who maintained that while population increases geometrically, food supply only increases arithmetically.

Senator Jones votes for a bill to build a bridge in Senator Smith's state. Senator Smith then agrees to vote for a bill that will lower alcohol taxes in Senator Jones's drunken state. Name the political term, often associated with pork barrel legislation that describes such an agreement.

First built in 1948 and originally called the Broadcaster, its name was changed after copyright disputes. Used by rock stars like Bruce Springsteen, Sheryl Crow, and Keith Richards, Jimmy Page of Led Zepplin played this type of instrument for the solo on "Stairway to Heaven." For 10 points -- name this guitar.

In the early Bolshevik era, he was arrested twice for subversion. After the 1917 revolution, he worked at the provincial level before becoming secretary of the Central Committee. Due to his support for Stalin, he became foreign minister and represented Soviet interests in the Allied conferences during World War II. For 10 points -- who was this namesake of a cocktail?

It leaves the Pennsylvania station, from track 29, at a quarter to four, and it's in Baltimore by the time I've read a magazine. Luckily for me, I've got just enough money to board. And when it arrives at my destination in Tennessee, a girl's waiting to hear I'll never roam again. For 10 points -- name this train I'm riding, the title of a Glenn Miller song.

This man greatly improved the invention of Niccolo Zucchi (ZOOK-kee), and in correspondence with John Flamsteed he dismissed the notion that comets have polarity. The flattening of the Earth at the poles was first suggested by this man, whose De motu corporum in gyrum (JIGH-rum) contained a new derivation of Kepler's third law. This man famously settled a celestial mechanics dispute between Robert Hooke and Edmond Halley by offering a proof of the inverse square law. Significantly advancing astronomy with his 1668 reflecting telescope, name this man who successfully explained the elliptical orbits of planets with his theory of universal gravitation in his book Philosophiae (fee-loh-soh-FEE-ay) Naturalis Principia (prin-SI-pee-uh) Mathematica.

This leader defeated Gerard de Ridefort and Roger de Moulins at the Battle of Cresson before they could negotiate with Raymond III of Tripoli. This leader had first gained power when his uncle Shirkuh died two months after ending the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt. He won a major victory a year after the death of Baldwin the Fifth over forces that included Knights Templar. That victory over King Guy [gee] at the Battle of Hattin allowed this leader to then take over Jerusalem. Name this founder of the Ayyubid dynasty who kept control of Jerusalem during the Third Crusade.

This leader first gained prominence as the sponsor of Aristophanes' (air-uh-STAHF-uh-nees) The Persians at the Dionysus (die-uh-NIGH-sus) Festival. He then served as the deputy of Ephialtes (eh-fee-AHL-tees) and helped decrease the power of the Areopagus (air-ee-oh-PAY-gus) noble council. After Ephialtes was assassinated, this leader gained power and used it to pay jury members and limit citizenship to people with two Athenian parents. This leader then encouraged the development of the Acropolis, especially the Parthenon. Name this leader associated with the Golden Age of Athens who Thucydides (thoo-SIH-duh-dees) called "the first citizen of Athens".

Some historians claim that this war started when metal workers under Constantino Davidoff planted a flag, though he disagrees. At the beginning of this conflict, Rex Hunt was captured and replaced as Governor by General Mario Menendez. Secretary of State Haig tried at first to mediate this conflict, but the United States eventually sided with Britain. This began with Operation Rosario and ended with the capture of Port Stanley and the South Sandwich Islands, which added to the popularity of Margaret Thatcher. Name this 1982 invasion by Argentina.

One reason this bill was passed was as a reaction to Orders in Council, and another reason was an incident involving James Barron and Salusbury Pryce Humphreys. The second major attempt to repair this bill led to a false promise to repeal the Berlin and Milan Decrees made by Napoleon. Passed after the Chesapeake-Leopold Affair, attempts to repair this bill included Macon's Bill Number Two and the Non-Intercourse Act. This unpopular act harmed the economy and was satirized in a political cartoon featuring a turtle. Name this 1807 act signed by Thomas Jefferson which restricted ships involved in trade.

This city includes a Buddhist temple on a pond called Benten-do (BEN- ten-doh), and its tallest building will soon be its Sky Tree. One of the tourist destinations in this city used to be called Big Egg City. One site in this city has had a hotel built on it three times, the second one being a Frank Lloyd Wright design in the shape of the letters I and H. This city also contains a slightly larger version of the Eiffel Tower. Name this city which contains an Imperial Palace built on the site of Edo Castle, the capital of Japan.

Historians debate whether or not hundreds of years ago this city had an African American community called New Guinea located near Copp's Hill. Copp's Hill has this city's second oldest cemetery, with the oldest at King's Chapel Burying Ground. This city has historical reenactments at its Old South Meeting House, and it contains a grasshopper weather vane on top of a building funded by Peter Faneuil (FAAN-yul). The oldest public park in the United States is this city's Common, which is also the beginning of its Freedom Trail. One neighborhood in this city, Charlestown, contains Breed's Hill and Bunker Hill. Name this capital of Massachusetts.

This leader put down a counterrevolution by commanding his future brother-in-law Joachim Murat, who later put down the Second of May Uprising. This leader defeated Count von Bennigsen at the Battle of Friedland a few months after a less decisive outcome at Eylau, leading to his Treaties of Tilsit with Russia and Prussia. He had already defeated Prussia at the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt, where his army captured Carl von Clausewitz. This leader would later win the Battle of Borodino and enter Russia, but he eventually had to retreat, and his later loss at Leipzig ended the War of the Sixth Coalition. Name this General who was then exiled to Elba and later lost at Waterloo, the Emperor of the French.

This President supported the Mann-Elkins Act, which allowed the Interstate Commerce Commission to regulate telecommunications, and he suffered a drop in popularity when Alaskan claims involving coalmines were interfered with by his Interior Secretary Richard Ballinger. This President was a strong supporter of the 16th amendment creation of an income tax, which passed at the end of his term. Name this man who finished third in his re-election effort behind Wilson and Teddy Roosevelt in 1912, but eight years later was appointed Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.

This country's Carlos Manuel de Céspedes (SAY-spay-days) tried to declare its independence, leading to the Ten Years' War. Julio Antonio Mella was assassinated after fleeing this country, which was blamed on this country's President Gerardo Machado. One of the revolutionaries who opposed Machado, Ramón Grau, would later become President, but a few years after his retirement this country was taken over in a coup led by Fulgencio Batista. Batista fled the country in 1959 after losing the Battle of Santa Clara to forces led by Che Guevara. Name this island nation that since 1959 has been run by Fidel Castro and his brother Raúl.

The first monarch of this kingdom generally is considered to be Kenneth the First of the House of Alpin. A dispute over its throne in the 13th century after the death of Margaret, Maid of Norway was known as the Great Cause and resulted in the ascension of John Balliol. Most of this region was known as Fortriu and inhabited by Picts, and it was also known as Caledonia, consisting of most of the region north of Hadrian's Wall. One of this kingdom's greatest victories was at the Battle of Bannockburn under the leadership of Robert the Bruce. Name this kingdom that in 1707 united with England to form Great Britain.

When writing about this topic, Joseph Schumpeter supported the work of Nikolai Kondratiev but disagreed with Simon Kuznets. These have been blamed on the Accelerator Principle, a form of positive feedback. Saltwater economists like the Keynesians advocate government action to counteract them, while freshwater economists claim they are a series of short-term phenomena that can be exacerbated by government action. Some economists claim that these are timed politically with troughs following elections and peaks leading into elections. These deviations from long-term growth alternate between expansions and contractions. Name this phenomenon that consists of booms and busts.

People who held this position for less than a year were called suffects, and there were 25 such people in the year 190 CE under Commodus and Cleander. People had to be at least forty-two years old to be eligible for this postion, and some military tribunes were given the power of this office during the Conflict of the Orders. Eventually, the praetors assumed the judicial powers of the holders of this office, which was first assumed by Lucius Junius Brutus and Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus in 509 BCE. Only holders of this office could propose laws, and each of these was given command over an army, though their powers decreased with the rise of Augustus. Name this office which was held by two people each year during the Roman Republic.
